## Done, and Not Finished

- The study has every hard part behind it
    - A question, a theory, and a reliability-tested codebook
    - A defensible sample, a clean dataset, three figures, and a test from Week 13

A study scattered across a dozen files is raw material. Tonight gives it a form.

## A Report That Rebuilds Itself

- The ordinary way to write up a study is quietly fragile
    - Run the analysis, copy the numbers, screenshot the figures, write around them
    - Change one coding rule and every pasted number is stale
    - Nothing in the document tells you so
- The alternative: put the analysis inside the document
    - A **Quarto document** interleaves prose with live code chunks

## Numbers You Never Type

```markdown
The analysis dataset held `r nrow(analysis)`
coded messages, of which `r n_labeled` carried
a gaming-status label.
```

- `n_labeled` comes from a chunk above the sentence:

```r
n_labeled <- analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(is_gaming)) %>%
  nrow()
```

In the rendered report those backtick expressions become the actual counts, so nothing in
the sentence can fall out of date.

## Figures You Never Paste

```r
#| label: fig-msglen
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Message length by channel type."
#| fig-alt: "YOUR TURN: what this chart shows."

analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(is_gaming)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(message_length, fill = is_gaming)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  v2v::theme_v2v()
```

Those lines sit inside an `{r}` chunk in the report, so the figure is produced at render
time rather than pasted in.

## Two Payoffs That Matter

- The report cannot drift from the analysis, because the report is the analysis
- The report can be checked
    - Anyone with the source files and the data renders the same results (Peng, 2011)

## One Click Renders It

- The idea predates Quarto and R: Knuth named it literate programming in 1984
- Here the "one click" is **Quarto: Preview** (**Ctrl+Shift+K**, **Cmd+Shift+K** on a Mac)
- It **renders**: it runs every chunk and builds the finished page

## IMRaD, and What Each Section Owes the Reader

- **Introduction:** the question and why it matters, built from your Research Proposal
- **Methods:** what was done, in enough detail for someone else to repeat it
- **Results:** what was found, without interpretation
- **Discussion:** what the result means, plus the honest limits

An abstract goes in front, and the references at the back.

## The White Paper, Specifically

- IMRaD structure, one citation style used consistently
- Effect sizes, confidence intervals, and power statistics, not only p-values
    - A model write-up for each test: [Chapter 13](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v/chapters/chapter13.html)
- A pre-registration disclosure in the Methods
- A Discussion that situates the finding in your theoretical literature

Converting your results into IMRaD costs something. Ask what is lost in the conversion, and what must be added.

## Methods, Three Transparency Markers

1. A **data provenance** statement: where the data came from, the date range, and what was excluded and why
2. A **reliability** report: the statistic, its value, the procedure, the threshold, and the single-coder limitation named as such
3. The **pre-registration disclosure**: the dated file in your project repository, cited by path and commit, and every departure from it

Each marker signals that the study meets the standard it claims. Any analysis beyond the
plan is labeled **exploratory**.

## What Preregistration Is For

> "Preregistration distinguishes analyses and outcomes that result from predictions from
> those that result from postdictions."
>
> Nosek et al. (2018, p. 2600)

- Preregistration is not a promise of virtue. It makes one distinction legible: what was planned and what was found afterwards
- Draft your disclosure sentence tonight
    - List every departure from your plan, and say how you report each one

## Where the 200 Points Sit

- **Introduction and framing:** 25
- **Methods:** 55
- **Results:** 40
- **Discussion:** 40
- **Abstract and references:** 15
- **Reproducibility and publication:** 15
- **Reflection:** 10

Methods carries the most weight because it carries the three transparency markers.

## One File per Row

| Template file | Rubric row |
|:--|:--|
| `01-introduction.qmd` | Introduction and framing |
| `02-methods.qmd` | Methods |
| `03-results.qmd` | Results |
| `04-discussion.qmd` | Discussion |
| `index.qmd` and `references.qmd` | Abstract and references |
| `05-reflection.qmd` | Reflection |

## Introduction and Framing, 25

- The question, why it matters now, and the gap
- Your theoretical lens, and one rival lens that predicts something else
- Each research question or hypothesis, traceable to the theory section

## Methods, 55

- Unit of analysis, population, frame, sampling method, and corpus size with its reason
- How the codebook was built, and the wrangling steps in plain words
- The three transparency markers, each under its own heading in `02-methods.qmd`
- Without all three, Methods cannot reach full credit

## Results, 40

- Descriptive statistics for every coded variable
- One test per research question, each with its effect size, confidence interval, and power
- One robustness check: the same question tested another reasonable way
- Two figures and one table, numbered, captioned, given alt text, and named in your text

## Discussion, 40

- The findings read through your lens and the rival lens
- Significance and size, kept apart
- The limits, including the single coder
- What a second coder would have added, and which finding is most at risk

## The Last Three Rows

- **Abstract and references, 15:** 150 to 250 words; fifteen sources, ten of them peer-reviewed studies; one style, used throughout
- **Reproducibility and publication, 15:** it renders, every number comes from the code, and it is live
- **Reflection, 10:** what was harder than expected, what the data could not answer, and what you would change

## Two Discussion Moves

- **Show interest** in what another person said
    - "Your point about sample size changes how I read this result"
- **Ask them to say more**
    - "What in the statement makes you think that?"

A comment that only agrees gives the room nothing new to answer.

## Exercise: Not Only a Threshold {.discuss}

[Wasserstein and Lazar (2016)]{.eyebrow}

> "Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on
> whether a p-value passes a specific threshold."
>
> Wasserstein and Lazar (2016, p. 131)

The word doing the work in that sentence is *only*.

- The result: gaming messages average 28.5 characters, non-gaming 33.7; *p* below .001, Cohen's *d* = -0.13
- For a reader who ignores the *p*-value, which number shows whether the gap matters?

## Your Questions on the Statement

[Wasserstein and Lazar (2016)]{.eyebrow}

- Ask a question you brought about the statement, or one that came up tonight
- A good question has more than one defensible answer
    - When is a result too small to be worth reporting?
- Answer the last speaker before you add a new point

## Rate Your Own Discussion

[Scale adapted from Tara Lineweaver, Butler University]{.eyebrow}

- **4:** the room knows more because of something I said
- **3:** I asked a question, and other people answered it
- **2:** I spoke, mostly to agree or to repeat a point
- **0:** I added nothing tonight
- Name one classmate whose comment changed your thinking

This rating has no points.

## One Book, Many Chapters

```yaml
project:
  type: book
book:
  title: "Your White Paper's Title"
  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - 01-introduction.qmd
    - 02-methods.qmd
    - 03-results.qmd
    - 04-discussion.qmd
    - 05-reflection.qmd
    - references.qmd
  appendices:
    - appendix-codebook.qmd
```

## One Book, Many Chapters (cont.)

- `_quarto.yml` lists the chapters in order
- The template wrote it for you, with your codebook as the appendix
- Open `_quarto.yml` in the `white-paper` folder in the **Explorer** panel and change the words after `title:` and `author:`

## Going Live

```r
v2v::deploy_portfolio(project)
```

- Run it from the Chapter 14 starter, Step 13; `project` is your White Paper folder's name, set in Step 2
- Commit and push first ([guide 12](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc501/12-commit-and-push-with-git.html)), or the second check stops it
- When it asks **Publish to GitHub Pages? [y/N]**, type `y` in the R terminal and press **Enter**
- Click by click: [Publish Your Site](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc501/13-publish-your-site.html)

## What Going Live Prints

```
── Pre-flight checks ──
ℹ No renv.lock found - skipping renv check
✔ no uncommitted changes
✔ _quarto.yml valid
──────────────────────
✔ Rendering 9 pages
Publish to GitHub Pages? [y/N] y
✔ Publishing to GitHub Pages
ℹ Published to https://your-username.github.io/your-repository/
✔ Portfolio live on GitHub Pages.
```

- You type the `y` in the R terminal, after you commit and push ([guide 12](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc501/12-commit-and-push-with-git.html))

## The Three Pre-Flight Checks

- **renv in sync:** the site is built with the package versions the source declares, checked only when the project has a `renv.lock`
- **No uncommitted changes:** every change is committed in **Source Control** ([guide 12](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc501/12-commit-and-push-with-git.html)), not only saved with **Ctrl+S** (**Cmd+S** on a Mac)
- **`_quarto.yml` valid:** the render will not fail partway through

Each check heads off one demoralizing failure, the worst being a collapse the night the
portfolio is due. The checks exist so the last step of a long study is the calm one.

## The Poster

- Appropriately large, in landscape: 48 by 36 inches recommended, 36 by 24 accepted
- Title, authors, and institution, plus a 100-word abstract
- Background and hypotheses, then the methods in condensed form
- Key results, with one or two `theme_v2v()` figures
- Discussion and implications, plus a QR code to your pre-registration or portfolio

## Your Poster Template

- `poster-template.pptx`, in the `white-paper` folder: one PowerPoint slide, 48 by 36 inches
- A box for each block, with its type size already set
- Replace each box's text with that block's short version from your paper
- Add your chart and QR code: [Build Your Conference Poster](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc501/18-build-your-conference-poster.html), Parts 1, 3, and 4

## The Poster, Block by Block

| Block | From the paper |
|:--|:--|
| Abstract | The abstract, cut to 100 words |
| Background and hypotheses | Two or three sentences, then each hypothesis |
| Method | What you studied, how many, how you coded it |
| Key results | The chart for your main test |
| Result and effect size | The sentence that reports your main test |
| Discussion and limitation | What it means, and the limit your paper names |

## One Study, Three Forms

- **The site:** your paper at a public address, where anyone can read and check it
- **The PDF:** the same paper as a document, for a client or a conference submission
- **The poster:** the study at a glance, for a conference session
- All three come from the same files, so a fix in one place reaches the site and the PDF on the next render

## What Earns Space on a Poster

- A poster is a ninety-second pitch, not a paper at a larger font
- Pick the one figure that lands the finding in thirty seconds, and give it the most space
- Cut every sentence that shows effort rather than result
- Numbers survive the cut. Hedges do not

Your reader is standing up, holding a drink, four feet away.

## Studio Block Two: Poster

- Sketch the layout on paper first, in blocks, before opening any software
- Place your chosen figure, then build the text around it
- Write the 100-word abstract last, once the blocks exist
- Generate the QR code from the URL the deploy gave you
- Read your title aloud, and cut it if it takes two breaths

## Common Failures in the Last Week

- The site renders on your machine and nowhere else, because renv drifted
- A figure vanishes from the site, because its chunk uses an object that exists only in your console
- The poster is exported at screen resolution and printed at full size, so it is blurry
- The QR code points at a private repository

Test the whole chain tonight, on a machine you did not build it on.

## The Reflection

- One paragraph, and the portfolio is incomplete without it
    - What turned out harder than expected
    - What the dataset could not answer, and why
    - What a second attempt would change
- Avoid both the bland version ("it went well") and the anxious version ("it all went wrong")

A reflection is evidence of judgment, not an apology.

## Checkpoint Before You Leave

You should have:

- A portfolio site that renders locally with no errors
- A Results section with zero hand-typed numbers
- A published URL, and a QR code pointing at it
- A poster layout with its main figure chosen and placed
- The reflection paragraph drafted, even roughly

## From Vibes to Variables

- A question became a design, and the design became data
- The data became figures and a test
- All of it became a site another person can check and extend
- The shared example happened to be Twitch chat. Nothing in the method depended on that, and your own study proves it

The distance from vibes to variables is the whole of research methods, and you have now
walked it once.
